Which batch is this sample from?

2 · Why it’s hard

The imaging varies more than the material.

Six sites, three co-registered detectors, native 25 nm pixels, each centred on a Si-rich particle. Edge width runs 52–90 nm and mean grey shifts from −2.5 to +3.3 between sites — acquisition differences a model can latch onto long before it sees the material.per-site stats: outputs/clean/summary.csv
3 · The trap

The obvious model learns the microscope, not the material.

Intensity-only model
0.71
Same electrode, slightly brighter image
Batch 1 ✓ → Batch 3 ✗
The best score in the room is a brightness knob away from nonsense. So we made a rule: nothing we build may read grey levels — only the microstructure itself.scripts/demo_confound.py
4 · The amount

We measured everything. The batches are chemically identical.

51 KPIs from two independent segmentation pipelines — silicon fraction, particle sizes, porosity — and not one tells the batches apart. Whatever separates them is hiding deeper than composition. That is the mystery the rest of this talk solves.outputs/kpis · analytical_benchmarks

6 · The twist

The 34 “sites” are crops of 13 parent electrodes.

We stitched the dataset back together: 17 seams, z ≥ 5.6, zero false positives across 2,108 wrong pairings. One parent spans several “batches”, and two of the three round-1 images abut crops whose organiser-released label is different (fn0mhxef has a single confirmed neighbour) — the label follows the crop, not the material. This is why validation is leave-one-parent-out.full figure & method: outputs/stitching/
7 · The model

NASA’s pretrained MicroNet — inside our pipeline.

Pretrained by NASA.
Engineered by us.

Its embeddings, never fine-tuned — our patch pipeline, our head, our parent-aware validation, our KPI-level explanations.

Leave-one-parent-out: accuracy 0.71 · p = 0.005.
